title: Thoughts on using AI to learn the basics as a newbie? (Is this considered vibe coding)
author: jesseblackman6710
selftext:
Hey. So some background, i have 0 coding experience and game dev experience.  And i started learning both by experimentation and some courses like "GDscript from zero". 

But i noticed myself using AI in my project to help me out to figure which functions should i use and what goes where. Like for example i know in my head that i need to make something that interact when touching something else. But i simply don't have the knowledge to translate that to code so i have AI help me. But to be clear, i don't blindly copy the code, i make him explain everything, i try to redo the code later to check if i still have it stored in my brain, and i try to debug myself a bit before giving up and looking it up. 

So am i harming myself in the long-term and "vibe coding" or am i using AI in a beneficial educational way?

(Also any course/youtube recommendations to improve my skills are welcome)

comments.author: wllmsaccnt
comments.body:
Most developers learned their skills in exactly the same way, just with different tools.  Before AI you'd do the same thing with stack overflow, blog posts, official documentation and forum / reddit threads.

The only difference is that AI makes this faster and more personalized; it's a better experience in almost every way.

Just make sure you keep verifying what the AI is telling you. They are reasonably accurate, but sometimes they are wrong about how to generalize concepts and new techniques and technology.

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: Could you elaborate more on the service model? I just use plain chatGPT 5.

replies.author: wllmsaccnt
replies.body:
For example, Claude Opus 5 has a terrible conversational style, but they improved it for Opus 5.5.

I can't give you advice on ChatGPT. I'd just say, don't be afraid to try out models from several different providers and figure out which one helps you learn easily from. You might find the one that is the best at writing code isn't the best at explaining solutions in a way you understand. 

For local models, if that is relevant for you, I wouldn't try to learn from anything smaller than Qwen's 27B model. Even then you'd probably be better off paying for a service for learning. It's awesome watching what modern open models can do locally, but there is still a large gap in knowledge between local and large hosted models.

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: Got it. I really appreciate the comprehensive replies. Thank you ❤️.

replies.author: dougthebuffalo
replies.body:
Just wanted to hop in and thank you for a much more reasonable take than OP got over on the indiegames sub.

Used correctly, AI is just as good as a personal tutor. If you learn from it and actually validate what it's teaching you, it's a perfectly fine way to learn the skills.

replies.author: wllmsaccnt
replies.body:
I've been a dev since before Stack Overflow existed. I feel mixed on AI tooling overall. It makes learning so much easier; I am jealous of people learning today compared to back when I was l making my first attempts (with published books). But...I miss the act of manually writing code. With the way AI coding agents work, my time is better spent on organizing the repo, establishing conventions, and reviewing user experiences.

I don't feel any dissonance from saying that LLM based AI and AI agents are amazing tools that people should be using to automate their work and learn from...while also feeling I would personally be happier if they never existed.

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: Yeah I'm glad i posted it to multiple subs as the view on AI seems so polarizing black/white with little in-between. But reading the different takes is helping me formulate my own opinion.

comments.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
comments.body:
I found that the interactive aspect of ai was amazing for helping me learn what I wanted to know without any extra info cluttering the process.
Youtube video tutorials sometimes don't tell me the little stuff I want to know.
I found it to be my favorite troubleshooting tool to learn to work in godot.
I also use it to generate my code. But by no means am I ignorant to the contents of the scripts. Every script gets revised, expanded, refactored for a constantly evolving idea of what I want to learn, and expand on next.... I'm learning with ai and. Frankenstein project. It's been fun

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: Glad to see you having success!

comments.author: jmontanholi
comments.body: Also, would 100% recommend checking some of codemonkey videos, he has one on C# that teaches from basic to advanced, and the concepts he teaches can be used in any language and platform. I am an experienced software developer, but had no experience in game dev, his videos helped me have a much better grasp of how things work.

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: This might be a dumb question but will i benefit if i mainly use GDscirpt? (It is like python apparently)

replies.author: jmontanholi
replies.body: So, he does videos for C# and Unity, while it might not translate 100% for your use case, it is still good game dev knowledge overall, because it will teach you concepts that you can use on whatever language/engine. So I'd still take a look, maybe skip some more technology specific parts, focus on the logic side of things

comments.author: Ok-Object7409
comments.body:
Very bad. AI is a terrible learning tool for a beginner.

A few points:

* You are unable to correct its mistakes.

* AI will lead you into a certain coding style.

* AI will prevent you from struggling. In the process of learning, you WANT to struggle. Working your way through problems is how you learn to effectively problem solve.

I always say this: AI is a tool for people who already know or have a reasonable idea of how to code. It is better to learn from it when you already understand the subject, not when everything is a mystery.

Whether you copy paste or not, doesn't really matter.

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: Thanks for the lengthy reply my guy! I appreciate it.

in a word, Crunch. However things have improved on that end of the industry as it stopped being the games industries dirty secret and the fans found out. now many studios advertise themselves as "no crunch studios" due to how endemic it was.

comments.author: -Star-Walker-
comments.body: Don’t use AI to learn coding. Use tutorials. Understand (!) what you are doing, try modify stuff, then try own stuff … maybe just a character walking in a room …

comments.author: HurryOne
comments.body: I learn from Ai by asking "why" questions and not "how" questions. Have it explain stuff to you instead of doing stuff for you.

replies.author: jesseblackman6710
replies.body: Good idea

replies.author: Sylvonara
replies.body: Yeah, it's all about what you ask/prompt, and course correct when needed. I started out with a project for work (nothing to do with game dev) and said "help me code.." and my mind was blown when Claude quickly just did all the coding and sent me the completed files without much needed from me other than testing, haha. So you can then give feedback to slow it down and explain how it all works so you can learn to replicate that type of stuff yourself.
